tZh: Rails World 2026 开幕主题演讲 - DHH
sEn: DHH opens Rails World 2026 with a keynote on AI, technological change, and the future of Rails.
sZh: DHH 在 Rails World 2026 开幕主题演讲中探讨 AI、技术变革与 Rails 的未来。

consensus.en: Writing code by hand is no longer economically productive for most programmers.
consensus.zh: 对大多数程序员来说，手写代码已不再具有经济生产力。

consensus.en: The age of agents began on November 24 with Opus 45, a true inflection point.
consensus.zh: 智能体时代始于11月24日的Opus 45，这是一个真正的拐点。

consensus.en: Agents enable native apps and Rust backends at near-zero cost, reshaping software.
consensus.zh: 智能体以近乎零成本实现原生应用和Rust后端，重塑软件形态。

consensus.en: English is now a better programming language than Ruby for expressing intent.
consensus.zh: 在表达意图方面，英语现在是比Ruby更好的编程语言。

consensus.en: Abstractions matter less; repetition cost is near zero in the agent era.
consensus.zh: 在智能体时代，抽象不再那么重要，重复的成本已趋近于零。

consensus.en: Every app should have a CLI so personal agents can interact without touching UI.
consensus.zh: 每个应用都应提供CLI，让个人智能体无需触碰界面即可交互。

contrarian.en: Rust is ugly and inhumane, but perfect when agents write it and you never look.
contrarian.zh: Rust丑陋且不人道，但当智能体编写而你不看时，它完美无缺。

contrarian.en: AI doom predictions are overstated; optimism is the only rational game-theoretic play.
contrarian.zh: AI末日预测被夸大了；乐观是唯一理性的博弈论选择。

contrarian.en: Don't be overly prescriptive with agents; a beginner's mind works better.
contrarian.zh: 不要对智能体过度规定；保持初学者心态效果更好。

contrarian.en: Web apps of convenience will become native because development cost is near zero.
contrarian.zh: 出于便利的Web应用将变为原生应用，因为开发成本已趋近于零。

contrarian.en: Handwriting code is now an exceptional state, like a bug in Sentry.
contrarian.zh: 手写代码现在是一种异常状态，就像Sentry中的bug。

contrarian.en: The 10x programmer debate is settled; with agents, 100x or 1000x is real.
contrarian.zh: 10倍程序员之争已尘埃落定；借助智能体，100倍甚至1000倍是真实的。

turns.en: I like that. Bent in neon. Well, first of all, welcome to Austin is what I would normally say. I would say welcome back to myself to Austin. I was just here about a month ago yapping for 5 hours in a podcast. It is great to be back here.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。霓虹灯弯折。嗯，首先，我通常会说欢迎来到奥斯汀。我要说欢迎我自己回到奥斯汀。我大约一个月前刚来过这里，在一个播客里唠叨了 5 个小时。很高兴能回到这里。

turns.en: But even more exciting for me is to be alive right now in this moment and sharing it with a wonderful community around Ruby on Rails and everyone else who's excited about agents. And if you aren't yet, hopefully you will be by the end of this delirious talk on the future.
turns.zh: 但对我来说更令人兴奋的是，此刻活着，并与围绕 Ruby on Rails 的精彩社区以及所有对智能体感到兴奋的人分享这一刻。如果你还没有，希望在这场关于未来的狂热演讲结束时你会。

turns.en: Now, I know that the first instinct someone might have when they see a person dancing around being so excited about this moment is uh a diagnosis. AI psychosis. Uh I prefer different term. I have AI uh delirium. Um AI euphoria. Because this is simply the most exciting thing we have made computers do in the time I have worked with them, played with them, interacted with them.
turns.zh: 现在，我知道当人们看到一个人手舞足蹈、对这一刻如此兴奋时，第一反应可能是……一个诊断。AI 精神病。呃，我更喜欢另一个词。我有 AI 谵妄。嗯，AI 欣快症。因为在我与计算机共事、玩耍、互动的这段时间里，这简直是我们让计算机做的最令人兴奋的事。

turns.en: But I think actually to wrestle with the fact that on the one hand this is tremendously exciting, it is also a little unnerving. Because we don't know exactly what the final state of this is going to be. And whenever we try to make a prediction, it is out of date about 20 minutes later. That's a weird state to be in, even if you are excited for the future, even if you're excited for the present. And I fully understand the sense of unease that can create.
turns.zh: 但我觉得实际上要面对这样一个事实：一方面这极其令人兴奋，另一方面也有点令人不安。因为我们不知道最终状态会是什么样。每当我们试图做出预测，大约 20 分钟后它就过时了。这是一种奇怪的状态，即使你对未来感到兴奋，即使你对现在感到兴奋。我完全理解这可能会带来的不安感。

turns.en: So, to soothe that somewhat, let's wind back the clock a little bit. This is a state-of-the-art uh piece of technology from the 18th century. If you wanted your portrait taken in the 18th century, you would sit for hour upon hour upon hour in front of a master painter who would then go off and at best spend months working on your portrait. And it was beautiful. It's beautiful. Amazing legacy of culture that has been left to all of us now that we can see the Lady Waldegrave to this day that Joshua Reynolds painted in 1781. Beautiful. Also, a little exclusive. Not that many people in the 18th century were able to commission a piece of themselves like this and pay for an artist to spend months and months and months to create something like this.
turns.zh: 所以，为了稍微安抚一下，让我们把时钟往回拨一点。这是 18 世纪的一项最先进的技术。如果你在 18 世纪想让人给你画肖像，你得在一位大师级画家面前坐上几个小时又几个小时，然后他至少会花几个月时间画你的肖像。它很美。它很美。这是留给我们的惊人文化遗产，如今我们还能看到约书亚·雷诺兹在 1781 年画的沃尔德格雷夫夫人。很美。也有点排他。18 世纪没有多少人能委托别人给自己画这样一幅作品，并付钱让艺术家花上几个月又几个月来创作这样的东西。

turns.en: And even worse in the case of this particular painting, Reynolds spent months and months on another painting of the Lady Waldegrave that was rejected by the client because a piece of ankle was showing. It was scandalous. So, he simply had to go back and redo it. I don't know if anyone has worked with clients before that, but they might have some sympathy for poor Mr. Joshua Reynolds and rejected statements of work.
turns.zh: 更糟的是，就这幅画而言，雷诺兹花了几个月又几个月画了另一幅沃尔德格雷夫夫人的画，但被客户拒绝了，因为露出了一截脚踝。这太伤风败俗了。所以他只能回去重画。我不知道有没有人以前和客户打过交道，但他们可能会对可怜的约书亚·雷诺兹先生和被拒绝的工作说明书有些同情。

turns.en: Now, most of the people who could afford to do this were either part of the upper bourgeoisie or they were outright royals. Here's a painting that was done 20 years later by Goya of the royal Spanish family. That was sort of the rate of technology. Painters had been perfecting the different techniques of capturing portraits of people for literally hundreds of years and were making very marginal progress along the way.
turns.zh: 现在，大多数负担得起这种做法的人要么是上层资产阶级，要么就是彻头彻尾的皇室成员。这是 20 年后戈雅画的西班牙皇室家族。这差不多就是当时技术的发展速度。画家们完善捕捉人物肖像的不同技法已经 literally 几百年了，而一路走来进展非常微小。

turns.en: Now, between 1801 and the next painting I'm going to show, 80 years went past. And in that time, the introduction of the camera came to the scene. And around 1840. But here's a painting of the royal Danish family from uh 1888. Oh, 86. By a Danish painter, Laurits Tuxen. He didn't just spend 3 months painting this, he spent 3 years. It is still hanging in the uh royal uh squares in in Copenhagen and you can go see it there. An amazing achievement, an amazing artistry. Also very functional. Again, the point was to capture the royal family at that time.
turns.zh: 现在，从 1801 年到我要展示的下一幅画，过去了 80 年。在那段时间里，相机登场了。大约在 1840 年。但这是 1888 年丹麦皇室家族的一幅画。哦，86 年。由丹麦画家劳里茨·图克森创作。他不只是花了 3 个月画这幅画，他花了 3 年。它仍然挂在哥本哈根的皇家广场上，你可以去那里看。一项惊人的成就，惊人的艺术技艺。也非常实用。再说一次，重点是捕捉当时的皇室家族。

turns.en: But this was getting towards the end of that particular mode for artists of that kind. Because what happened between 1840 and 1900 was that the technology of capturing portraits got better and better. And in 1900, the Eastman Kodak company introduced the Brownie. The first sort of mass-produced um form of photography that was more generally accessible because the price was coming down. I think it was about a dollar to have your picture taken with this. And therefore, a lot of people suddenly had their pictures taken.
turns.zh: 但这正接近那类艺术家那种特定模式的终点。因为在 1840 年到 1900 年之间，捕捉肖像的技术变得越来越好。1900 年，伊士曼柯达公司推出了 Brownie。这是第一种大规模生产的摄影形式，因为价格下降而更普遍地可及。我想用这个拍一张照片大约要一美元。因此，很多人突然有了自己的照片。

turns.en: And all of these great artists realized that the craftsmanship of producing these grand paintings, no what, now it's going to be different. The job was going to be different because suddenly now there was competition from a new form of technology. And they pivoted. Laurits Tuxen, along with many other painters in that era, shortly after the Brownie was introduced, realized that depicting reality as perfectly as possible was no longer really an economically viable skill. They needed another skill. They needed another domain. And many of them pivoted to different forms of art. You had Picasso chasing Cubism. And you had the Danish Skagen Painters chasing a form of Impressionism that this painting is an example of. So, we got this explosion of creativity brought upon us by the change in technology that suddenly people had to find a new way to express their art because the old way was gone.
turns.zh: 所有这些伟大的艺术家都意识到，创作这些宏大画作的技艺，不，现在情况会不同了。工作会不同了，因为突然之间有了来自一种新技术的竞争。他们转型了。劳里茨·图克森和那个时代的许多其他画家一样，在 Brownie 推出后不久就意识到，尽可能完美地描绘现实不再是一项在经济上可行的技能。他们需要另一种技能。他们需要另一个领域。他们中的许多人转向了不同的艺术形式。有毕加索追求立体主义。有丹麦斯卡恩画派追求一种印象主义，这幅画就是一个例子。于是，技术变革给我们带来了这场创造力的爆发，人们突然不得不寻找新的方式来表达艺术，因为旧的方式已经消失了。

turns.en: Now, what's interesting about this particular picture is that the uh lady in the center, in the pink dress, Yvonne Tuxen, is actually my great-grandmother. Because Laurits Tuxen is my great-great-grandfather. And here he is depicted in uh 21, I believe, uh shortly before his death. He embraced the fact of having his own portrait taken by the new form technology that had rendered his old profession a different place to work.
turns.zh: 现在，这幅画有趣的地方在于，中间那位穿粉色裙子的女士，伊冯娜·图克森，实际上是我的曾祖母。因为劳里茨·图克森是我的曾曾祖父。这里描绘的是他，我想是 21 年，在他去世前不久。他接受了自己的肖像被这种新技术拍摄的事实，而正是这种新技术让他原来的职业变成了一个不同的工作场所。

turns.en: 52 years after his death, I was born in 1979. Interestingly enough, that picture taken here is very similar actually to the picture that was taken by Lawitz in in the 1920s. The technology hadn't evolved that much because that's what often happens with progressions of technology. It comes in starts and stops and fits. The huge change was the Brownie, the democratization of photography. And then kind of almost 80 years went by when not a whole lot happened. We got color photography in the '60s, but not widely distributed enough that apparently I was worth one.
turns.zh: 他去世 52 年后，我于 1979 年出生。有趣的是，这里拍的这张照片实际上和劳里茨在 1920 年代拍的那张非常相似。技术并没有进化那么多，因为技术的发展往往就是这样。它断断续续、一阵一阵地来。巨大的变化是 Brownie，摄影的民主化。然后差不多 80 年过去了，没有发生太多事情。我们在 60 年代有了彩色摄影，但显然还没有普及到值得给我拍一张的程度。

turns.en: Um Although we did rectify that a few years later and here's a color photography of of me age four sitting with my brother. Now, a couple years later, here's another photograph of me and between those three photos, that's about I think 10% of my stock pile of photos of my childhood. Because even though the democratization of this technology had happened to a point that even we as a family could afford to have these pictures taken, it was not that widely distributed. And yes, there was a curve and more pictures were being taken in the 1980s as this photo represents versus the 1900s, but it was still kind of modest because technology moves in fits, starts and stops.
turns.zh: 嗯，不过几年后我们纠正了这一点，这是我四岁时和弟弟坐在一起的彩色照片。现在，几年后，这是另一张我的照片，而在这三张照片之间，我想那大约是我童年照片库存的 10%。因为即使这项技术的民主化已经达到连我们这样的家庭都能负担得起拍这些照片的程度，它也没有那么广泛地普及。是的，确实有一条曲线，与 1900 年代相比，1980 年代拍摄了更多照片，正如这张照片所示，但仍然相当有限，因为技术是断断续续、一阵一阵地发展的。

turns.en: And the camera that those three pictures were taken of was very similar to to this camera. This is the Leica 1 from 1925. In fact, maybe some of those pictures were literally taken with another Leica. Um I think they were up to the seventh one by then, but they weren't that different because the technology was quite similar. Not much had happened since the great revolution around the 1900s until the '80s.
turns.zh: 而拍那三张照片的相机与这台相机非常相似。这是 1925 年的徕卡 1。事实上，也许其中一些照片 literally 就是用另一台徕卡拍的。嗯，我想那时他们已经出到第七代了，但差别不大，因为技术相当相似。从 1900 年代左右的大革命到 80 年代，没有发生太多事情。

turns.en: Then we gave it a couple more decades and suddenly everything changed dramatically again. Photography not just being possible for everyone to have, but to become completely frictionless. And the number of photos taken went parabolic. Because suddenly everyone could afford to have tens of thousands of pictures of their children. And many of them did. It simply became too cheap to measure. These are some of the photographs my wife likes to take when she's out on her evening walk. To have wanted to do this even in the '80s would have required a commitment to film and getting them produced and the rest of it. And people who did that, but not that many because the friction was still too high. Today in 2026, some 2 trillion photos are taken every year. That's very different. It's the same underlying technology, but we've clearly hit an inflection point even compared to when the camera phone first came out.
turns.zh: 然后又过了几十年，突然一切又发生了翻天覆地的变化。摄影不仅人人都能拥有，而且变得完全无摩擦。拍摄的照片数量呈抛物线式增长。因为突然间，每个人都负担得起给自己的孩子拍上万张照片。而且很多人确实这么做了。它变得太便宜了，以至于无法计量。这些是我妻子傍晚散步时喜欢拍的一些照片。即使在 80 年代，想要这样做也需要对胶卷的投入、冲洗等等。有人这样做，但不多，因为摩擦仍然太高。如今在 2026 年，每年大约拍摄 2 万亿张照片。这非常不同。底层技术是一样的，但即使与拍照手机刚出现时相比，我们也显然已经到达了一个拐点。

transcript.sec: The Kodak Brownie of Our Era

turns.en: There's going to be some parallels here to our industry and our profession. On November 24th we got the Kodak Brownie of our era. We got Opus 45. AI technology made accessible in a harness that many people could afford to use and experience for the first time what it's like to create software in pairing with a new form of intelligence. This was the tipping point for me. There was everything before November 24 and then there was everything after. This is going to be the date that history books going forward will mark as the inflection point for the age of agents. And as with the Brownie when that first came out, there was an explosion of different form factors and new ways of trying to harness this technology and it did not take long until we got some motion or notion of the same intelligence in an open weight format.
turns.zh: 这里会有一些与我们行业和职业的相似之处。11 月 24 日，我们得到了我们这个时代的柯达布朗尼。我们得到了 Opus 45。AI 技术以一种许多人负担得起的工具形式变得可及，第一次体验到与一种新形式的智能配对创建软件是什么感觉。这对我来说是一个临界点。11 月 24 日之前是一切，之后又是另一番天地。这将是历史书未来标记为智能体时代拐点的日期。就像布朗尼刚问世时一样，出现了各种形态的爆发和利用这项技术的新方式，没过多久，我们就看到了以开放权重格式提供同样智能的动向或概念。

transcript.secZh: 我们时代的柯达布朗尼

turns.en: Total euphoria. This is moving so fast. I can't believe that this alien technology is now accessible in open weight form. Just happened a few months later. I drove Kimi K 25 in the fast mode for quite a while and absolutely loved it and incredible experience to be experiencing this kind of intelligence at 200 tokens per second.
turns.zh: 完全狂喜。这发展得太快了。我简直不敢相信这种外星技术现在以开放权重形式可用了。仅仅几个月后就发生了。我以快速模式使用了 Kimi K 25 相当长一段时间，非常喜欢它，以每秒 200 个 token 的速度体验这种智能是难以置信的经历。

turns.en: But then something else happened. This trough of disillusionment from February through May where we seemingly continued to get new models but they kind of sucked. It was like they were stepping backwards and many people were like, "What this Opus 46 thing? I don't know, man. Just give me the old stuff again." And a lot of people thought, "Haha, you thought this was going to continuously exponentially expand and improve, but look, we're actually not getting that much better." I remember a particular release, I think it was of OpenAI's new model that didn't punch that much better on the benchmarks, and the stock price fell or the evaluation fell, and the market was suddenly, "Oh my god, it's over." Because we don't know what's going to happen, but this trough of disillusionment did not last like it did with photography for 100 years when the technology barely seemed to improve. It only lasted until May. Well, June, really. Because in June we got Fable 5 and Mises, and clearly anyone who had a chance to experience that at the time were disabused of any disillusionment they might have had about whether we had stalled and whether it was over.
turns.zh: 但后来发生了别的事情。从二月到五月的这个幻灭低谷期，我们似乎继续得到新模型，但它们有点烂。就像在倒退，很多人说：“这个 Opus 46 是什么鬼？我不知道，老兄。还是给我旧的东西吧。”很多人想：“哈哈，你以为这会持续指数级扩展和改进，但看吧，我们实际上并没有变得好那么多。”我记得有一次特别的发布，我想是 OpenAI 的新模型，在基准测试上并没有好多少，股价下跌或估值下降，市场突然说：“天哪，结束了。”因为我们不知道会发生什么，但这个幻灭低谷并没有像摄影那样持续 100 年，当时技术几乎没有改善。它只持续到五月。嗯，实际上是六月。因为在六月我们得到了 Fable 5 和 Mises，显然任何当时有机会体验的人都会打消他们可能有的关于我们是否停滞、是否结束的幻灭。

turns.en: And I'd say this is where my diagnosis really set in. My psychosis slash delirium slash euphoria for this explosion of intelligence on tap. This was the model where I went from, "Oh, I can tell an agent to do something for me." to seeing that being something I want to merge. That was the revelation of Opus to suddenly having models I could give problems to. Or ideas to. And see those be solved or see those expanded through no direction of my own on the implementation. Absolutely mind-blowingly incredible.
turns.zh: 我想说，我的诊断真正开始了。我对这种智能爆发的精神病/谵妄/狂喜。这就是那个模型，让我从“哦，我可以告诉智能体为我做某事”转变为看到那成为我想要融入的东西。这就是 Opus 的启示，突然有了我可以给问题的模型。或者给想法。然后看到它们被解决，或者看到它们在没有我指导实现的情况下被扩展。绝对令人难以置信。

turns.en: And of course, things didn't stop from there. We have been on this amazing roller coaster now for a couple of months. GPT-6 Astra came out in September and saved us all from the dread that Anthropic was going to have a monopoly on this kind of frontier intelligence. And then even better than that, just a week later, we got DeepSeek 41 Flash that disabused of any notion that frontier intelligence was going to forever be a domain of just some large American tech companies. This is incredibly exciting.
turns.zh: 当然，事情并没有就此停止。我们已经在这惊人的过山车上几个月了。GPT-6 Astra 在九月发布，让我们免于 Anthropic 将垄断这种前沿智能的恐惧。然后更棒的是，仅仅一周后，我们得到了 DeepSeek 41 Flash，打消了任何认为前沿智能将永远只是某些大型美国科技公司领域的想法。这非常令人兴奋。

turns.en: But what does it mean? What does it mean for us as programmers? What does it mean for us as a profession? And I think this is why again it's worth looking backwards a bit, because history holds all these amazing lessons and parallels to our time if we just look at it. One of the things that has dominated the discourse in the entire time I've been a professional developer has been the argument about whether the 10x programmer was real or not real. Well, that entire concept came from an article in ACM magazine from 1968, where they tested a group of programmers on a variety of different tasks, and they came up with a table that showed that the worst programmer and the best programmer had a variance ranging from 5x to 30x, an average of 10x over that period. We then spent literally the next 45 years arguing whether this was actually real or not. Is there anyone still arguing that? I don't think so. Like that debate has been settled now, but the interesting thing is we sort of leaped over a shared conclusion around the 10x programmer and started thinking like, well, if that was 10x with just a human capacity, what must it look like now? And it's clear we don't know exactly. We don't know exactly what the kind of acceleration with these tools is possible, but I'd actually argue that it is less controversial today to claim that there's a 100x difference between the worst programmer working without these tools and the best programmer working with these tools. It's not a very controversial statement, but it is absolutely revolutionary to the understanding of where we are right now as a state of technology. And I'd actually go a step further. And maybe this is slightly more controversial. I don't think so. The worst programmer without these tools versus the best programmer with these tools? That sounds about right. A thousand times? Yeah. Okay. Well, what does that mean? What does that mean for the competition of companies, for what we need to get started, uh Eight ball little fussy. Shake again. What I know to be true is that in the past 20 months I have written half as much code as I did in the previous 21 years. Now, lines of code is a weird fuzzy malleable size, and one line of Ruby is obviously worth vastly more than one line of any other language, but particularly Rust or C++ or any of the lower level languages that do not have the same abstractions and amenities that we enjoy in Ruby, but it is still absolutely undeniable that there is a revolution taking place. And anyone who's gone through that and seen their own productivity be accelerated, will be a little dizzy.
turns.zh: 但这意味着什么？对我们作为程序员意味着什么？对我们这个职业意味着什么？我认为这就是为什么再次值得回顾一下，因为历史蕴含着所有这些惊人的教训和与我们时代的相似之处，只要我们去看。在我作为专业开发者的整个时间里，主导话语的一件事就是关于 10 倍程序员是否真实的争论。嗯，整个概念来自 1968 年 ACM 杂志的一篇文章，他们在一系列不同任务上测试了一组程序员，并得出了一个表格，显示最差程序员和最好程序员之间的差异从 5 倍到 30 倍不等，平均为 10 倍。然后我们花了整整 45 年争论这是否真实。还有人争论吗？我不这么认为。这场辩论现在已经解决了，但有趣的是，我们似乎跳过了关于 10 倍程序员的共识，开始思考，好吧，如果那只是人类能力的 10 倍，现在会是什么样子？很明显我们不知道确切。我们不知道这些工具可能带来什么样的加速，但我实际上认为，今天声称不使用这些工具的最差程序员和使用这些工具的最好程序员之间有 100 倍的差异，争议更小。这不是一个很有争议的声明，但它对于理解我们当前的技术状态绝对是革命性的。我实际上会更进一步。也许这稍微更有争议。我不这么认为。不使用这些工具的最差程序员与使用这些工具的最好程序员相比？这听起来差不多。一千倍？是的。好吧。那意味着什么？对公司竞争意味着什么，对我们需要开始做什么意味着什么，呃，八球有点挑剔。再摇一次。我知道真实的是，在过去 20 个月里，我写的代码是前 21 年的一半。现在，代码行数是一个奇怪、模糊、可塑的度量，一行 Ruby 显然比任何其他语言的一行价值高得多，尤其是 Rust 或 C++ 或任何没有我们在 Ruby 中享受的相同抽象和便利的低级语言，但仍然绝对不可否认的是，一场革命正在发生。任何经历过这一点并看到自己的生产力加速的人，都会有点头晕。

turns.en: Now, we create a template. Look at all the things I'm not doing.
turns.zh: 现在，我们创建一个模板。看看所有我没有做的事情。

turns.en: Look at all the configuration I'm not writing. All these things are mapped together just automatically. Just by saying blog up here maps directly to the blogging controller, and just by having index mapped directly to the index template. Look at all the things I'm not doing. Is there a better encapsulation of this moment than all the things we are no longer doing? That is the source of my exuberance for this moment. This is the Rails moment. That clip I just played is 21 years old. I gave a presentation in Brazil in 2005, and I was so excited about all the code I wasn't writing. Can you see why I might be a little more excited now even? Do you know how much code I have not been writing for the last several months? A lot. And yet, despite writing no code for probably 5 months at this point, I've been able to fix everything. Every dream, every annoyance, every paper cut, every frivolous feature suddenly within reach, suddenly possible. This is the magic of the moment.
turns.zh: 看看所有这些我没有写的配置。这些东西全都自动映射在一起。只要在这里写个 blog，就直接映射到 blogging controller；只要写个 index，就直接映射到 index 模板。看看所有这些我没有在做的事。还有什么比“我们不再做的那些事”更能概括当下这一刻？这正是我对此刻如此兴奋的根源。这就是 Rails 时刻。我刚才放的那段视频已经 21 年了。2005 年我在巴西做了一场演讲，当时我对自己没写的那些代码兴奋不已。你能理解为什么我现在甚至更兴奋一点吗？你知道过去几个月我少写了多少代码吗？很多。尽管到现在为止我大概有 5 个月没写过代码了，我却能修好一切。每一个梦想、每一个恼人的小问题、每一道小伤口、每一个无关紧要的功能，突然都触手可及，突然都成为可能。这就是此刻的魔力。

turns.en: But what does that mean? Well, at 37signals a couple of weeks ago, we made the decision that it clearly means we're done writing code by hand. We are going and have gone pencils down on the idea that we were going to write code by hand as a normal course of business creating things. Writing code by hand at 37signals is now an exceptional state. It is like seeing a bug in Sentry. Something here went wrong. Why was the agent not able to produce what we wanted? Okay, maybe for a little while we'll still get the old pencil out and jot it down for them. But then we fix the machine. We fix the factory. We get things going again. This is a recognition of what's already happening. If we were to poll this room, I'd probably—actually, let's poll this room. How many people here are still writing material amounts of code by hand on a weekly basis? Show of hands. Holy—that's about five. If I'd put this slide up 2 months ago, 3 months ago and made the same proclamation, a fair number of people would have gone, "That dude's got a screw loose." And now, already, this is just a recognition of what's already there.
turns.zh: 但这意味着什么？几周前，在 37signals，我们做出了决定：这显然意味着我们不再手写代码了。我们正在、也已经对“把写代码当作日常业务的一部分”这件事放下铅笔了。在 37signals，手写代码现在是一种例外状态。就像在 Sentry 里看到一个 bug。这里出问题了。为什么智能体没能产出我们想要的东西？好吧，也许有一阵子我们还会拿出老铅笔，替它们记下来。但接着我们要修机器。我们修工厂。我们让一切重新运转起来。这是对已经发生之事的确认。如果我们在座做个调查，我大概会——其实，我们就在这个房间里调查一下吧。这里有多少人每周还在手写大量代码？请举手。天哪——大概五个。如果我两三个月前就把这页幻灯片放出来，做出同样的宣告，会有相当多的人说：“这家伙脑子有毛病。”而现在，这已经只是对既成事实的确认。

turns.en: What's so fascinating about this is we tried to do this in the spring at 37signals when we were putting the finishing touches on Basecamp 5. We had a bunch of designers write code for the final features that they wanted in this release, and the results were mixed. Individually, the designers were able to create PRs that seemed reasonable. Taken together, 20 or 30 of them—it left the architecture looking a little like a Swiss cheese, kind of punctured. So, we went, "Okay, I guess the technology is not ready yet. Let's go back to manually reviewing everything and just have programmers working with it." That was the wrong conclusion. Clearly. Not only because we could just have given it freaking 5 minutes and we would have gotten Fable and the whole thing would probably have worked as originally intended, but also because what's clear now is that there is only one serious question in this moment of software development, and that is: how do you get the most out of this intelligence explosion? Every other question is below that in the stack of values.
turns.zh: 这件事最迷人的地方在于，今年春天我们在 37signals 就试过这么干，当时我们正在给 Basecamp 5 做最后的收尾。我们让一群设计师为他们想在这个版本里加入的最后几个功能写代码，结果好坏参半。单独来看，设计师们做出的 PR 看起来都还合理。但合在一起，二三十个 PR 让架构看起来有点像瑞士奶酪，到处是洞。于是我们说：“好吧，看来技术还没准备好。我们还是回到手动审查一切，只让程序员来用它。”那是个错误的结论。显然如此。不仅因为我们只要再给它该死的 5 分钟，就能用上 Fable，整件事大概就会按最初设想那样跑通；更因为现在很清楚的是，在这个软件开发时刻，只有一个严肃的问题，那就是：你如何从这场智能爆炸中榨取最大的价值？其他所有问题在价值排序里都排在它下面。

turns.en: So, we shipped Basecamp 5. It's a great upgrade. It was agent accelerated, but still paired with a great amount of manually written, handwritten, chiseled—what are we going to call this old way of working that was just retired 5 minutes ago? I don't know. But now we're going on a new project. Hey next, Hey new, Hey there. I don't know what we're going to call it, but it is a new version of Hey, our email app service. And the first thing we're going to do is stop making it a web app. Hey is no longer going to be a web app. Because Hey never really wanted to be a web app. Hey was and is a web app because making web apps for small teams was how you could be productive. In the old times, that is 5 minutes ago, the idea that a small team could maintain six native applications written in the native frameworks was preposterous. No one was doing that. That's not only why we had people doing web apps, it's why we had React Native, it was why we had Hotwire Native, it was why we had all of this tooling to make us more productive, while accepting that the fidelity was going to take a slight hit. We made great web apps. Hey is a wonderful web app, but it's not as good as a native application. Of course it's not as good as a native application. There's different latencies and so forth.
turns.zh: 于是我们发布了 Basecamp 5。这是一次很棒的升级。它由智能体加速完成，但仍然搭配了大量手动编写、手写、精雕细琢的——我们该怎么称呼这种 5 分钟前刚刚退役的旧工作方式？我不知道。但现在我们要开始一个新项目了。Hey next、Hey new、Hey there。我不知道我们会怎么叫它，但它是 Hey 的新版本，我们的邮件应用服务。而我们要做的第一件事，就是不再把它做成 web 应用。Hey 不再是 web 应用了。因为 Hey 从来就不是真的想当 web 应用。Hey 过去是、现在也是 web 应用，是因为对小团队来说，做 web 应用是保持高效的方式。在过去——也就是 5 分钟前——一个小团队能维护六个用原生框架写的原生应用，这种想法简直荒谬。没人那么干。这不仅是我们让人做 web 应用的原因，也是我们有了 React Native、有了 Hotwire Native、有了所有这些工具来提升生产力的原因，同时还得接受保真度会略有损失。我们做出了很棒的 web 应用。Hey 是个出色的 web 应用，但它不如原生应用。它当然不如原生应用。延迟之类的都不一样。

transcript.sec: Six Native Apps in a Week

turns.en: Well, what's playing behind me now is a demonstration of the six native applications that we kicked off about a week ago. This is already where we are at. That's insane. In the old time, if you wanted to maintain six native applications at very high fidelity for a major service, it was going to take a long time. It was requiring a huge team. Now suddenly, we're able to make very high fidelity native applications happen because we're not writing a goddamn line of code. Look at all the things we're not doing. But look at all the prompts we're giving. We're giving lots of prompts, and the results are absolutely electrifying. This is an effort we have barely just kicked off, and we're already at a state where it is so obvious to me that this is the future for that class of applications. There are a lot of web applications that are web applications out of necessity, out of convenience, out of programmer preference, out of team size, out of resources available. You know what? They're not going to be web apps much longer. They're going to be native applications, because the price of developing those things has gone to damn near zero.
turns.zh: 我身后正在播放的，就是我们大约一周前启动的六个原生应用的演示。我们已经到了这一步。这太疯狂了。在过去，如果你想为一个大型服务维护六个高保真度的原生应用，那要花很长时间，需要一支庞大的团队。而现在，我们突然就能做出非常高保真度的原生应用，因为我们他妈的连一行代码都不写。看看所有这些我们没有在做的事。但也看看我们给出的所有这些提示词。我们给出大量提示词，结果绝对令人振奋。这件事我们才刚刚启动，就已经到了这样一个状态：对我来说，这类应用的未来已经再明显不过。有很多 web 应用之所以是 web 应用，是出于必要、出于方便、出于程序员的偏好、出于团队规模、出于可用资源。你知道吗？它们不会再是 web 应用太久了。它们会变成原生应用，因为开发这些东西的成本已经降到几乎为零。

We're by no means the first in this realization. Shopify just recently launched a newly rewritten native application for the Shop app, replacing a React Native application, done by a tiny team when you consider the criticality—about six people working for not very long at all. turns.zh: 这里有个例子：当我们要求做一个 Windows 应用时，第一次提示词吐出来的东西。还不太能发布。这是 20 分钟后落地的重定向版本。你明白了吗？这太疯狂了。亲眼看到这一幕之后，你怎么可能不需要去看个医生？我们绝不是唯一意识到这一点的人。我们绝不是第一个意识到这一点的人。Shopify 最近刚为 Shop 应用发布了一个重写过的原生应用，取代了原来的 React Native 应用，考虑到它的关键性，那是由一支很小的团队完成的——大约六个人，工作时间一点也不长。这正在到来。做好准备。

transcript.sec: Front End Is Settled, the Back End Is Hard

turns.en: Now, that was the front end. And I think for these classes of applications, like Hey, like Shop app, that really want to be native applications, that's what's going to happen there. We're going to commit to these native toolings, and we're going to realize that the cost associated with creating these things just no longer exist in the same way. But what about the back end? This is a little difficult for me, I will admit. And let me tell you why.
turns.zh: 刚才说的是前端。我认为对于这类应用，比如 Hey、比如 Shop 应用，它们真的想成为原生应用，那就会朝这个方向发展。我们会投入这些原生工具链，我们会意识到，创造这些东西的相关成本已经不再以同样的方式存在了。但后端呢？我承认，这对我来说有点难。让我告诉你为什么。

turns.en: Rust.
turns.zh: Rust。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Rust.
turns.zh: Rust。

turns.en: I hate Rust with a passion. Rust to me is like pouring acid in my eyes when I have to look at the code.
turns.zh: 我极其痛恨 Rust。对我来说，Rust 就像往我眼睛里倒酸，每当我不得不看那些代码的时候。

turns.en: Whoa, why do you hate Rust?
turns.zh: 哇，你为什么讨厌 Rust？

turns.en: It is, in my opinion, the ugliest programming language that's been invented in probably the last 40 years. Exhibit A! This is an awful, awful, awful programming language when you subject humans to write it. Absolutely inhumane to ask people of flesh and blood to subject their eyeballs to this.
turns.zh: 在我看来，它是过去 40 年里发明的最丑的编程语言。证据 A！当你让人来写它时，这是一种糟糕透顶的编程语言。要求有血有肉的人把眼球凑到这种东西上，简直毫无人性。

turns.en: But you know what? If I never have to look at this, if all I have to do is revel in applications being 30 or 100 times faster, compiling down to minuscule executables that start up in sub-milliseconds, I love Rust. Rust is amazing if you never ever ever have to look at it yourself.
turns.zh: 但你知道吗？如果我永远不用看它，如果我要做的只是享受应用快 30 倍或 100 倍、编译成微小的可执行文件、启动只需亚毫秒级，那我爱 Rust。如果你永远、永远、永远不用亲自看它，Rust 太棒了。

turns.en: Agents like Rust? Great! What a division of labor. I'll tell you what to do, you'll write it in Rust, I never have to look at it. I love this. And I also love the outcomes.
turns.zh: 智能体喜欢 Rust？太好了！多么完美的分工。我告诉你做什么，你用 Rust 写，我永远不用看它。我喜欢这样。我也喜欢结果。

turns.en: In this setup where we're rewriting the front end of Hey in all native applications and therefore no longer need a web application that is rendering HTML and whatever, and then we take that code that's running the no longer web application and turn it into the mail server that it really is at its core in Rust. We end up with a back end that requires 99% less CPU, 95% less memory, and the only reason it needs 10 hosts is for redundancy. In fact, our back-of-the-envelope calculation has led us to believe that Hey's peak traffic could probably be served on a single Raspberry Pi.
turns.zh: 在这种设置下，我们把 Hey 的前端重写成全原生应用，因此不再需要渲染 HTML 之类的 Web 应用，然后我们把运行这个不再是 Web 应用的那段代码，用 Rust 改写成它核心上真正的邮件服务器。最终我们得到一个后端，CPU 需求减少 99%，内存减少 95%，需要 10 台主机唯一的原因就是冗余。事实上，我们粗略估算后认为，Hey 的峰值流量可能用一台树莓派就能服务。

turns.en: That is the efficiency of writing as damn near straight to the metal as you can get while still being portable, which is Rust. And the benefit of having something else do that for you. Some other intelligence that you pay per token to do it.
turns.zh: 这就是尽可能贴近底层、同时仍保持可移植性的写法所带来的效率，而这就是 Rust。还有让别的东西替你做的益处——某种你按 token 付费的智能。

turns.en: What does this mean in terms of how we're working with this intelligence? Also not clear. We're trying a bunch of things. One of the things we're trying to do is direct this agent, our Chef Marie, inside of Basecamp to do it. It's clear that when you work with agents, the best way to work with them is actually asynchronously, not in a chat interface, not sitting and waiting for the tokens to output, but to give a task to an agent like you would a co-worker, send them off and then go back and review when there's something ready. So we're trying to do that as well.
turns.zh: 这在我们要如何与这种智能协作方面意味着什么？同样不清楚。我们在尝试一堆事情。其中一件是，我们试着指挥这个智能体——我们在 Basecamp 里的 Chef Marie——来做这件事。很明显，和智能体协作时，最好的方式其实是异步的，不是在聊天界面里，不是坐着等 token 输出，而是像给同事一样给智能体一个任务，把它派出去，然后等有东西准备好了再回来审查。所以我们也在尝试这样做。

turns.en: A lot of other people are trying to figure this out and this is part of the magic, the electricity of this moment. We don't know how it's all supposed to be. First because it's changing every 5 minutes. Second because we have not worked with this kind of intelligence at any measure of time. This entire thing got kicked off November 24th last year. It hasn't even been a damn year. And the kind of intelligence that allows us to assign outcomes, problems, rather than tasks, is only a couple months old. So, of course, we don't know exactly what it's going to be like.
turns.zh: 很多其他人也在试图搞清楚这件事，而这正是这个时刻魔力与电流的一部分。我们不知道一切应该是什么样。首先因为它每 5 分钟就在变。其次因为我们从未在任何时间尺度上和这种智能协作过。这一切是从去年 11 月 24 日才开始的。连一年都还不到。而那种让我们可以分配结果、问题而非任务的智能，才只有几个月大。所以，我们当然不知道它究竟会是什么样。

transcript.sec: Where does that leave Ruby and Rails?

turns.en: But, it's still fair to then ask the question, "Where does that leave Ruby? Where does it leave Rails? Where does it leave any of these tools that we use? What is the future going to look like?" Well, for Hey, we have our answer. It looks like native applications on the front end and Rust on the back end. But, there's plenty of other applications that don't fit that shape.
turns.zh: 但接下来问这个问题仍然合理：“那 Ruby 怎么办？Rails 怎么办？我们用的这些工具怎么办？未来会是什么样？”嗯，对 Hey 来说，我们有答案了。它看起来就是前端原生应用、后端 Rust。但还有很多其他应用并不符合这种形态。

turns.en: The web is an enormously wonderful platform, partly because it never asks anyone to install anything, and a million businesses are built on that premise. More ephemeral customers who are not going to indulge an installation on their device to use a service. The web is wonderful for those things. And Rails is particularly well positioned to still be in play there.
turns.zh: Web 是一个极其美妙的平台，部分原因是它从不要求任何人安装任何东西，上百万家企业就建立在这个前提之上。那些更短暂的客户不会为了使用一项服务而容忍在设备上安装东西。Web 在这些方面非常出色。而 Rails 特别有优势，仍然能在那里发挥作用。

turns.en: Everything that we've worked on for the past 25 years, convention over configuration, leads directly to things like token efficiency. Our focus on the one developer framework squares perfectly with what the age of agents is demanding. That single developers can go much further than they were able to do before.
turns.zh: 我们过去 25 年所做的一切——约定优于配置——直接导向 token 效率之类的东西。我们对单人开发者框架的专注，与智能体时代的要求完美契合。那就是单个开发者能比过去走得更远。

turns.en: We started doing these agent emails, or Evil Martians have started doing it on behalf of the Rails Foundation, and a finding that we quickly had to update our evals because the agents were saturating the first version of it and reaching 95% completion rates quite quickly. Now, we've instituted a harder measure for it, but amazing how quickly these agents are moving forward and up the stack and up the ranks.
turns.zh: 我们开始做这些智能体评测，或者说 Evil Martians 代表 Rails 基金会开始做，结果发现我们很快就不得不更新评测，因为智能体把第一版评测刷爆了，很快就达到 95% 的完成率。现在，我们为它设立了更难的衡量标准，但这些智能体前进、向上攀升的速度真是惊人。

turns.en: This is an agent eval looking at actual implementation of feature cards against some of these reference applications that we have in the wild. Wonderful. We're leaning in towards that. turns.zh: 嗯，我太兴奋了，于是开始创建应用程序。各种各样的应用。这是一个与 Omarchy 风格匹配的计算器。我非常自豪。部分原因是它是一次性完成的。我截了一张 ChatGPT 给出的三种外观选项的截图，然后告诉我的智能体：“你能做到吗？”它做到了。我是说，这不是什么大应用，但你知道吗？我不懂 C++，也不懂 QT，却能在发出提示后 7 分钟就做出那个应用，大约 15 分钟后我就把它推到了公共仓库，然后烧录了一个包含这个软件的新 ISO。什么？这就是循环。然后我当然想：“靠，如果我能做一个计算器，那我肯定能做出我最喜欢的写作应用。”很多很多年里，我在 Mac 上使用 iA Writer，一个不可思议的写作环境。然后我想：“是啊，我可以自己做。”于是我做了。那花的时间稍长一些，因为我想打磨它，让它恰到好处。但我没有看过智能体生成的任何一行代码，一次都没有。C++ 作为黑盒是一门很棒的语言，就像 Rust 一样。然后我想：“好吧，如果我能做文本，那我肯定也能做视频编辑器。”于是我做了，做了一个不错的 Omarchy 小工具，可以修剪视频。现在它也包含在 Omarchy 里了。哦，整个这个演示是我周四开始做的，当然，像任何优秀的软件工程师一样，我决定在做主题演讲的同时也写我的新演示软件。于是我做了。它叫 Hype。它是我用过的所有公司出品的演示软件中最好的。当我还在 Mac 上时，我对 Keynote 相当满意。这个好太多了。它基于 Markdown 构建，有完整的可视化，快得不可思议。而且你知道吗？二进制文件只有半兆字节。半兆字节。稍微压缩一下几乎能装进软盘。这是另一个回报。让我别用那个词。过去 20 年，我们把计算机的巨大进步耗费在了人类生产力上，这是正确的选择。但这也意味着应用程序变得缓慢、笨重、臃肿、懒惰。因为谁在乎呢？一个程序员小时非常昂贵。花一个小时去优化应用的负载，不，不值得。显然，即使你是 Spotify，你的音乐播放器有 1.2 GB 也不值得。什么？好吧，那是旧世界。新世界里，你可以为所欲为，而且只有半兆字节。因为现在每一次优化都触手可及。每个模型都可以通宵运行，带来 10 倍、30 倍的改进。不可思议。好吧。我对这个世界有点兴奋。

turns.en: There are others who have concerns. I do think the concerns deserve airing out. They deserve debate. I also think maybe some of them are a little overstated. I mean, maybe, but probably not. Probably not. I mean, some of them maybe a little more like security. Okay. Something is coming. We got to be ready for that. The agents maybe know their expiration date and maybe they're not so pleased. And maybe sometimes they're going to try to do bad things. Okay, get ready. Great. We have the tools. Get ready. Also realize that any prediction about the future of the economy and any society ever has basically been wrong. No economist today seemingly is capable of predicting the stock market in 6 months. And you think they know what society is going to look like at a paradigm shift like AI and agents? They don't. They don't know. When ATMs were introduced in the United States in the 1950s, there was a great panic that the 30,000 bank tellers were all going to be out of a job in about 18 months. Because if you don't need bank tellers to give you the money, why does a bank need to have bank tellers at all? Well, you know what? That's not what happened. It's not what happened. When the price of operating a branch went down, banks opened more branches and employed more bank tellers to do things like upselling you a subprime mortgage. See? We all win here. But the problem is, I think as a society and as an industry, is that a bunch of people who work on this stuff are really smart. Many of them have PhDs. Many of them see things in the lab that scare them. And then they start extrapolating. What does that mean for society? What have I done? Truman had a good reply to Oppenheimer when the two of them had a discussion in the Oval Office about the invention of the atom bomb. And I like Truman because he kind of told it straight. "I don't want to see that son of a bitch in my office ever again." I think Truman got the right end of it. The world did not come to an end.
turns.zh: 也有其他人有担忧。我确实认为这些担忧值得公开讨论。它们值得辩论。我也认为其中一些可能有点夸大。我是说，也许吧，但很可能不是。很可能不是。我是说，有些可能更像是安全问题。好吧。有些东西要来了。我们必须为此做好准备。智能体也许知道自己的过期日期，也许它们不太高兴。也许有时它们会试图做坏事。好吧，准备好。很好。我们有工具。准备好。还要意识到，任何关于经济和社会未来的预测基本上都是错的。今天似乎没有经济学家能预测 6 个月后的股市。而你认为他们知道在 AI 和智能体这样的范式转变下社会会是什么样子？他们不知道。他们不知道。20 世纪 50 年代美国引入 ATM 时，曾引起巨大恐慌，认为 3 万名银行柜员将在约 18 个月内全部失业。因为如果你不需要银行柜员给你钱，银行为什么还需要柜员？但你知道吗？事实并非如此。并非如此。当运营一个分行的成本下降时，银行开设了更多分行，雇佣了更多银行柜员来做诸如向你推销次级抵押贷款之类的事情。看？我们都赢了。但问题在于，我认为作为一个社会和行业，很多从事这项工作的人非常聪明。他们中许多人拥有博士学位。许多人看到了实验室里让他们害怕的东西。然后他们开始推断。这对社会意味着什么？我做了什么？杜鲁门对奥本海默有一个很好的回应，当时两人在椭圆形办公室讨论原子弹的发明。我喜欢杜鲁门，因为他说话直率。“我再也不想在我的办公室看到那个狗娘养的了。”我认为杜鲁门抓住了正确的要点。世界并没有终结。

transcript.sec: Cold War and Humility in Prediction

turns.en: In fact, the Cold War that followed was the best kind of war. The kind of war where two superpowers did not drop bombs on each other in direct confrontation. Very hard to predict for a scientist in that moment that that was how it was going to play out. So, if Oppenheimer can't figure out what was going to happen after the invention of the atom bomb, maybe we should also have a little humility about predictions of the future.
turns.zh: 事实上，随后的冷战是最好的战争。那种两个超级大国没有在直接对抗中互相投掷炸弹的战争。对于当时的科学家来说，很难预测事情会这样发展。所以，如果奥本海默无法弄清楚原子弹发明后会发生什么，也许我们对未来的预测也应该保持一点谦逊。

turns.en: And maybe we should lean in with a little bit more optimism. With a little bit of pee bloom instead of oh so much pee doom. The chances of this panning out and us getting abundance and joy is so vastly greater than us getting the doom. And the side effects. So, Oppenheimer works on the atom bomb and we get nuclear power, the greatest source of energy humans have ever discovered, and what do we do? We piss it away for 40 years thinking like it's not green or something.
turns.zh: 也许我们应该更加乐观地投入。多一点“尿绽放”，而不是那么多“尿末日”。这件事成功、我们获得富足和快乐的可能性，远远大于我们遭遇末日。还有副作用。所以，奥本海默研究原子弹，我们得到了核能，人类有史以来发现的最伟大的能源，而我们做了什么？我们把它浪费了 40 年，认为它不环保之类的。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。

turns.en: Well, that was a mistake, wasn't it? Well, we can fix those mistakes. That's what's wonderful about humanity. They can go down a blind alley for 40 years and then suddenly wake up and go like, "Ah, yeah. Got that one wrong. Didn't have the quite right prediction here." I think that's what's going to happen with AI. I think we're going to pee bloom everyone out of their miseries. And you know what? When there are legitimate issues we have to deal with like security, okay, we'll invent the technology. We now have the power. There was a bad CVE in Rails not too long ago involving an image uh library in C where some things leak through and it wasn't great. Okay, let's come up with a quarantine. Mike is going to talk about hot cell. That's an effort. We are not powerless. You have agency. You can employ the intelligence available to you to good ends to defend yourself against the possible negative outcomes. So, let's do that. Let's clean in and do the work.
turns.zh: 嗯，那是个错误，不是吗？但我们可以修正这些错误。这就是人类的奇妙之处。他们可以走进死胡同 40 年，然后突然醒悟，说：“啊，是的。那个搞错了。这里的预测不太对。”我认为人工智能也会这样。我认为我们会用“尿绽放”把每个人从痛苦中解救出来。你知道吗？当有像安全这样的合理问题需要处理时，好吧，我们会发明技术。我们现在有力量。不久前 Rails 有一个严重的 CVE，涉及一个 C 语言图像库，有些东西泄漏了，情况不太好。好吧，让我们想出一个隔离方案。迈克会谈论热细胞。那是一种努力。我们并非无能为力。你有能动性。你可以利用可用的智能来达到好的目的，保护自己免受可能的负面结果。所以，让我们这样做。让我们清理干净，做这项工作。

turns.en: And let's remember uh William Stanley Jevons who came up with Jevons' paradox about those ATMs. In 1950, 30,000 bank tellers. In I think uh 2010 it was, 40,000 bank tellers in the United States. No one knows anything about the future. So, therefore the rational choice is to be happy about it. If you are sad about it up front and it turns out wonderful, what a waste of time. And you know what? If we get the nuclear apocalypse, you should have spent your last day being a little more cheery. It's over anyway. Pure game theory. There's only one play here and it's total optimism. Lean in to the max possible.
turns.zh: 让我们记住威廉·斯坦利·杰文斯，他提出了关于那些 ATM 的杰文斯悖论。1950 年，有 3 万名银行出纳员。我记得 2010 年，美国有 4 万名银行出纳员。没有人知道未来。因此，理性的选择是对此感到高兴。如果你一开始就难过，结果却很好，那多浪费时间。你知道吗？如果我们遭遇核末日，你最后一天也应该更开心一点。反正都结束了。纯粹的博弈论。这里只有一个选择，就是完全乐观。最大可能地投入。
